titre: The ecological parable that doesn't hold up to the evidence
accroche: Easter Island serves as a warning: a people who destroy their forest and collapse. The data say otherwise
contenu_vulgarise:
The story is familiar, and it has the shape of a fable. The inhabitants of Rapa Nui supposedly cut down their palm forest to erect and move monumental statues, exhausted their island, sank into famine and war, and collapsed before the Europeans arrived.

A lesson is drawn from it: this is what a society does when it consumes its environment without seeing the end coming. The island, isolated in the middle of the Pacific, is said to stand as a scale model of the Earth.

The parable is effective. Part of the archaeology done on the island seriously challenges it.

## What deforestation owes to rats

The disappearance of the palm forest is established. What is less so is that axes were the main cause at first.

The Polynesians did not land alone. The Pacific rat came with them, on the canoes, deliberately or not. On an island with no predators, a rat population grows explosively, and these rats eat palm seeds.

Nut shells that have been recovered bear characteristic gnaw marks. A forest whose seeds are eaten en masse no longer renews itself, whatever share humans may also have cut to build canoes or to extract the edible heart.

Recent work confirms this role of rats by combining it with human clearing, without making it the sole cause.

## What becomes of the collapse

The other piece of the story is demographic: a population that supposedly peaked very high before collapsing.

Recent reconstructions do not find this peak. They describe instead a population that rises and then levels off, adapted to an island impoverished in trees through suitable farming techniques: stone mulch gardening, gardens sheltered from the wind.

What actually collapsed the population of Rapa Nui is documented and dated: the diseases introduced after European contact, and the Peruvian slave raids of the 1860s, which deported a significant share of the inhabitants.

The collapse is real. It came after contact, and it was not ecological.

## Why the fable endures

The debate is not settled, and one certainty should not be swapped for another. Some researchers maintain the overexploitation thesis.

But the standard story's success does not rest on the strength of its evidence. It rests on what it says about us: a society that destroys itself through blindness is a useful lesson, and an isolated island makes a perfect metaphor.

What should hold our attention is the direction in which the story was built. No one started from the data and drew a moral from it. A parable was needed, and an island was recruited to carry it, at the cost, for its inhabitants, of becoming the people who killed themselves.

repere.texte: On an island with no predators, a pair of rats can produce several million individuals in a few decades. The palm nut shells found on Rapa Nui bear gnaw marks.
repere.source: Hunt & Lipo, “Ecological Catastrophe and Collapse: The Myth of ‘Ecocide’ on Rapa Nui (Easter Island)”

carte.punch: The Rapa Nui ecocide story owes its success to the parable, not to the strength of its evidence.
carte.idee: Easter Island serves as an ecological warning. But archaeologists dispute it: seed-eating rats played a key role in the loss of the forest, and the population collapsed after European contact, from disease and slave raids.

quiz.question: What collapsed the population of Rapa Nui?
choix: Introduced diseases and slave raids, after European contact
Famine following the disappearance of the palm forest
Wars between clans over control of the last resources
Soil exhaustion from poorly suited intensive farming
quiz.explication: The population collapse is real, dated, and came after contact: epidemics and deportations in the 1860s. Recent reconstructions do not find the population peak followed by famine that the standard story assumes, and describe instead a society stabilized by farming techniques suited to an island without trees.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role are Pacific rats thought to have played in the disappearance of the palm forest?
choix: They ate palm seeds, preventing the forest from regenerating
They gnawed directly at the trunks of adult palms until they fell
They spread a fungal disease that killed the palms
They were deliberately introduced to clear the forest
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On an island with no predators, the rat population grows explosively, and these rats eat palm seeds: a forest whose seeds are eaten en masse no longer renews itself, and recent work combines this role of rats with human clearing, without making it the sole cause.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do recent demographic reconstructions of Rapa Nui show, unlike the standard story?
choix: A population multiplied by ten just before the arrival of the Europeans
A complete disappearance of the population even before European contact
A population that rises and then levels off, without the peak followed by collapse in the standard story
Continuous growth, never interrupted up to today
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Recent reconstructions do not find the population peak followed by famine that the standard story assumes: they describe instead a population that rises and then levels off, adapted to an island impoverished in trees through suitable farming techniques.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what explains the success of the standard ecocide story, regardless of the strength of its evidence?
choix: It was confirmed without reservation by all the archaeologists working on the island
It rests on demographic data that have gone unchallenged since the 1950s
It was recently invented to discredit Polynesian peoples
It offers a useful lesson about collective blindness, and an isolated island makes a perfect metaphor
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The story's success does not rest on the strength of its evidence but on what it says about us: a society that destroys itself through blindness is a useful lesson, and an island isolated in the middle of the Pacific makes a perfect metaphor.
